paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning methods that adjust a probabilistic action policy to increase average reward. Natural-gradient methods make these adjustments using a mathematical description of the policy's geometry. The authors focus on two proposed descriptions, both expressed as Fisher information matrices, and note that existing natural-gradient algorithms had used only one of them.

Their generalized natural gradient interpolates linearly between the two matrices. This makes the choice of geometry adjustable rather than fixed. They then develop generalized Natural Actor-Critic, or gNAC, to estimate this gradient efficiently using estimating-function theory. A near-optimal auxiliary function reduces the variability of the gradient estimates, addressing the practical problem of learning from noisy information.

With an appropriate interpolation parameter, gNAC can be understood as an extension of the existing Natural Actor-Critic algorithm. Numerical experiments report efficient estimation of the generalized gradient and better performance than NAC. These findings support the proposed combination of flexible geometry and variance reduction in the tested settings.
neurips-2009-a-generalized-natural-actor.tldr: An adjustable natural-gradient geometry and variance-reduction method extend Natural Actor-Critic and outperform it in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Models of binary neural firing patterns describe which neurons fire together, but relating these patterns to continuous stimuli requires a broader model. This paper extends second-order maximum-entropy modeling to describe stimuli and population activity jointly. The construction constrains their joint second-order statistics, producing a Gaussian-Boltzmann distribution that combines continuous and binary variables.

The authors derive marginal distributions, which describe either part of the model separately, and conditional distributions, which describe one given the other. They report that fitting the model is a convex problem and that its computational complexity matches that of purely binary models. Thus, including continuous stimuli preserves useful computational properties of the existing framework.

The model also extends classical spike-triggered average and covariance analysis, providing a nonlinear way to identify stimulus features associated with a population's sensitivity. In the reverse direction, it can infer a distribution over stimuli from an observed neural response. This supports stimulus decoding and supplies a natural measure for comparing spike trains, connecting population statistics with the information those populations represent.
neurips-2009-a-joint-maximum-entropy-mod.tldr: A joint maximum-entropy model connects binary neural activity with continuous stimuli, supporting feature extraction, decoding, and spike-train comparison.

paragraphs: Estimating a large vector from random linear measurements can involve a complicated nonlinear optimization problem. This paper analyzes maximum a posteriori, or MAP, estimation with non-Gaussian models and Gaussian measurement noise. It uses the replica method from statistical physics, which the authors explicitly describe as non-rigorous, to study behavior as the problem dimension becomes large.

The central result is a decoupling description: the asymptotic behavior of the vector estimate can be represented through scalar MAP estimators. This replaces a coupled, high-dimensional performance analysis with simpler one-dimensional calculations. The analysis provides a MAP counterpart to earlier replica work on minimum mean-squared-error estimation.

The framework applies to compressed-sensing estimators including basis pursuit, lasso, thresholded linear estimation, and zero-norm estimation. For lasso, the scalar rule becomes soft thresholding; for zero-norm estimation, it becomes hard thresholding. Within the replica analysis, these reductions make quantities such as mean-squared error and sparsity recovery computationally tractable to calculate exactly. That computational benefit should be understood within the method's stated non-rigorous, asymptotic setting.
neurips-2009-asymptotic-analysis-of-map-.tldr: A non-rigorous replica analysis reduces large-system MAP estimation to scalar problems, enabling tractable compressed-sensing performance calculations.

paragraphs: A permutation test assesses a statistic against the distribution it would have under rearrangements of the data. Constructing that reference distribution can require substantial computation. This paper proposes a shortcut: approximate the permutation distribution using the Pearson distribution family, with the approximation determined by its first four moments.

The key contribution is a recursive method that derives those moments analytically, without actually performing permutations. Moments summarize features of a distribution, so the method uses a compact description to build an approximate reference distribution. This separates the calculation of the needed summaries from the potentially expensive process of generating rearranged datasets.

The authors demonstrate the approach with different test statistics on both simulated and real data. They report a combination of accuracy and efficiency from joining a nonparametric permutation-test foundation with a parametric distribution approximation. The distinction matters: the moments are derived theoretically, while the resulting permutation distribution is approximated. The contribution is therefore an efficient route to permutation-based inference whose practical accuracy is supported by the reported experiments.
neurips-2009-efficient-moments-based-per.tldr: Analytically computed moments allow Pearson distributions to approximate permutation-test reference distributions without performing permutations.

paragraphs: This paper develops a mathematical tool for analyzing loopy belief propagation, a message-passing procedure on graphs containing cycles. The authors connect the Hessian of the Bethe free energy to an edge zeta function. The Hessian describes local curvature, so the formula links the shape of an optimization objective with a graph-based mathematical object.

One application is a sufficient condition for the Hessian to be positive definite. The analysis also establishes non-convexity for graphs with multiple cycles. These results address different aspects of the same landscape: favorable local curvature does not imply that the entire objective is convex. Understanding that distinction helps interpret the behavior of an iterative inference procedure.

The formula further clarifies how local stability of a belief-propagation fixed point relates to local minima of the Bethe free energy. The authors also develop an approach to studying uniqueness and give several conditions under which a fixed point is unique. Together, these contributions provide tools for reasoning about local stability, objective geometry, and uniqueness as related but distinct questions.
neurips-2009-graph-zeta-function-in-the-.tldr: A formula linking Bethe free-energy curvature to a graph zeta function yields conditions concerning belief-propagation stability and uniqueness.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a family of probability distributions that describes data through a hierarchy of Lp norms. Each norm summarizes part of the input, and these summaries feed into further norms. The resulting Lp-nested symmetric distributions extend spherical and Lp-spherical models previously used to represent natural-image statistics.

The family includes Independent Subspace Analysis, or ISA, for suitable parameter and norm choices. This provides a common framework for exploring models between ISA and Lp-spherical symmetry. The authors describe the distributions as easy to estimate and show that, like related models, they permit a nonlinear mechanism for reducing dependence among variables.

Their main findings examine whether ISA's proposed independent groups actually separate dependencies in image features. Without contrast gain control, dependencies between these groups were stronger than dependencies among individual coefficients within a group. With contrast gain control, when ISA identified multiple groups, the filter responses were already almost independent. These findings make preprocessing central to interpreting the apparent independence structure, rather than treating the groups discovered by ISA as automatically independent.
neurips-2009-hierarchical-modeling-of-lo.tldr: Hierarchical Lp distributions unify image-feature models and reveal that ISA's dependence structure changes substantially with contrast gain control.

paragraphs: Markov random fields represent dependencies among variables through an undirected graphical model. Learning their parameters by maximum likelihood is difficult because the probability model includes a global normalizing constant. This paper studies an approximate learning approach that combines Robbins-Monro stochastic approximation with Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling.

The proposed improvement concerns how the sampling component explores the model's distribution. The authors use operators based on tempered transitions to better explore distributions with many distinct modes. This matters because parameter learning depends on the information supplied by sampling; exploring the distribution more effectively can improve the estimates used during learning.

The authors report considerable improvements in parameter estimates for large, densely connected Markov random fields. Results on MNIST and NORB demonstrate learning of generative models for high-dimensional, structured data, along with good performance on digit and object recognition tasks. The contribution connects an improvement in sampling behavior to practical model learning: tempered transitions make the stochastic approximation procedure more effective in the multimodal settings examined.
neurips-2009-learning-in-markov-random-f.tldr: Tempered-transition sampling improves approximate maximum-likelihood learning in large Markov random fields by exploring multimodal distributions more effectively.

paragraphs: Learning to rank uses relevance-labeled examples to learn how to order documents. A difficulty arises when the training objective differs from the measure used to evaluate the final ordering. This paper focuses on Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain, or NDCG, which depends on document positions rather than directly on the numerical scores a ranking function produces.

The authors propose a probabilistic framework that optimizes expected NDCG across possible document permutations. This turns the ranking measure into an objective defined through a distribution over orderings. To make that objective manageable, they introduce a relaxation that approximates the average over permutations and a bound-optimization procedure intended to make computation efficient.

The approach matters because it brings the training objective closer to the criterion used to judge retrieval quality. It addresses both the dependence on discrete ranks and the computation involved in considering many orderings. Experiments on several benchmark datasets report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art ranking methods, supporting the approach empirically in those evaluations.
neurips-2009-learning-to-rank-by-optimiz.tldr: A probabilistic approximation to expected NDCG aligns ranking training with its evaluation measure and improves reported benchmark performance.

paragraphs: This paper asks how accurately any method can estimate a high-dimensional regression function when only a small subset of variables matters. The function is assumed to be a sum of univariate components from a Hilbert space. Observations are independent, include white Gaussian noise, and have covariates whose components are independently drawn from a common distribution.

Using information-theoretic arguments, the authors derive tight minimax lower bounds for squared prediction error. The rate is governed by the larger of two difficulties. One is identifying the unknown subset of s relevant variables among p candidates, contributing s log(p/s)/n. The other is estimating the sum of s component functions, which depends on their function space but not on the ambient dimension p.

For an m-th order Sobolev space, the function-estimation term scales as s times n raised to −2m/(2m+1). This separates the cost of discovering relevant variables from the cost of learning their effects. Comparison with a particular l1-penalized approach shows that this approach can attain the minimax-optimal rate under the studied setting.
neurips-2009-lower-bounds-on-minimax-rat.tldr: Tight lower bounds separate sparse additive regression's difficulty into selecting relevant variables and estimating their component functions.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to reconstruct a low-rank matrix when only a small, randomly selected portion of its entries is observed and those observations contain noise. Low rank supplies the structure that makes reconstruction possible: the matrix has fewer independent directions of variation than a general matrix of the same size.

The authors analyze OPTSPACE, a previously introduced algorithm that combines spectral techniques with manifold optimization. Spectral techniques work with the matrix's underlying linear structure, while manifold optimization provides a way to optimize over structured candidates. The paper describes the algorithm as having low computational complexity, making the relationship between efficient computation and reconstruction quality central to the study.

Its main contribution is a set of proven performance guarantees that are order-optimal in a number of circumstances. This is a qualified optimality statement about how performance scales in those circumstances. The problem connects to collaborative filtering, structure from motion, and positioning, where useful information must be recovered from incomplete and imperfect measurements.
neurips-2009-matrix-completion-from-nois.tldr: OPTSPACE combines spectral methods and manifold optimization to recover low-rank matrices from noisy partial observations, with order-optimal guarantees in several circumstances.

paragraphs: A continuous-time Markov chain describes a system whose next state and time spent in each state are random. This paper asks for the most likely complete trajectory: both the sequence of states and the duration of each visit. That is a different inference task from determining the distribution of the system's state at a particular time.

The authors study three versions. The first fixes an initial state and asks for a trajectory up to a specified final time. The second also fixes the final state, requiring a trajectory connecting the two endpoints. The third allows only partial observation, paralleling trajectory inference in hidden Markov models.

A central finding is that a maximum-likelihood trajectory need not always be well-defined. The paper provides a polynomial-time test for this issue before addressing trajectory recovery. When well-definedness holds, all three versions can be solved in polynomial time using efficient dynamic programming algorithms. The result therefore supplies both a check that the requested solution makes sense and algorithms for finding it when that check succeeds.
neurips-2009-maximum-likelihood-trajecto.tldr: The paper tests whether most-likely continuous-time Markov trajectories are well-defined and, when they are, computes them in polynomial time.

paragraphs: Dyna planning uses a model to support reinforcement learning through simulated experience. This paper extends that architecture so its model can project states or features multiple steps into the future. The aim is to improve both policy evaluation, which estimates the value of a policy, and control, which seeks better action choices.

The first extension is a lambda-model that interpolates between one-step prediction and an infinite-step model. It can be learned efficiently online, allowing multi-step predictions to become part of ongoing learning. The second extension is a dynamic model for control that predicts the consequences of a sequence of greedy actions and can track the optimal policy over the long run.

Experiments report faster policy evaluation with multi-step models than with single-step models. For control, the dynamic tracking model is much faster than the tested model-free algorithms, and multi-step Dyna brings policies and value functions to their optima faster than single-step Dyna. These findings support using longer predictive horizons within the planning architecture.
neurips-2009-multi-step-dyna-planning-fo.tldr: Multi-step predictive models extend Dyna planning and accelerate policy evaluation and control in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Prediction often assumes that training and test examples come from the same distribution. This paper studies a setting where an adversary can influence the test inputs, breaking that assumption. The learner's model and the adversary's changes are treated as decisions in a prediction game, so the data distribution becomes part of a strategic interaction.

The authors consider single-shot games whose participants need not have exactly opposing costs. This allows the learner's objective and the adversary's objective to differ without requiring every gain for one to be an equal loss for the other. They identify conditions that ensure a unique Nash equilibrium and derive algorithms for finding the corresponding prediction models.

An equilibrium describes mutually compatible choices: neither participant improves its own objective by changing its decision alone while the other stays fixed. This makes equilibrium analysis relevant to prediction under strategically altered inputs. An empirical email spam-filtering case study explores properties of the resulting models, complementing the conditional theoretical results on existence of a unique equilibrium and its computation.
neurips-2009-nash-equilibria-of-static-p.tldr: The paper gives conditions and algorithms for unique Nash-equilibrium prediction models when an adversary can alter test-input distributions.

paragraphs: This paper explores how clustering can be expressed through a regression framework. The motivation is that regression offers a convenient place to introduce penalties that encourage desired statistical properties. The authors build on optimal scoring, an approach originally developed to express Fisher linear discriminant analysis as a regression problem, and extend its use to unsupervised learning.

The concrete result is a clustering algorithm called optimal discriminant clustering, or ODC. Its role is to demonstrate that the optimal-scoring perspective can support a learning task in which the groups are unknown. This moves the framework beyond its original use in discrimination and makes it a basis for constructing clustering procedures.

The authors also connect ODC with spectral clustering, discriminative clustering, and sparse principal component analysis. These connections place the new algorithm alongside established unsupervised methods and show how a regression-based perspective can relate different formulations. The stated contribution is a new approach to implementing and developing unsupervised algorithms, with ODC serving as its particular realization.
neurips-2009-optimal-scoring-for-unsuper.tldr: Optimal discriminant clustering adapts regression-based optimal scoring to unsupervised learning and connects it with several established methods.

paragraphs: EEG classification must cope with noise and artifacts in recorded brain signals. Common spatio-spectral patterns extend common spatial patterns by using delay embedding, incorporating delayed signal information into the filtering approach. Although the spatio-spectral method had shown advantages, the version discussed in this paper was restricted to problems with two classes.

The authors extend it to multiple classes through a theory of multiclass Bayes error estimation. Their method, called MCSSPs, chooses spatio-spectral filters by minimizing an estimated Bayes error that has a closed-form expression. This ties filter selection to an estimate of classification error and supplies a shared objective for the multiclass problem.

The distinction between estimated and actual Bayes error matters: the filters are optimized according to the proposed estimate. Experiments on the BCI competition 2005 dataset report significantly better EEG classification than previous multiclass common spatial pattern methods. The contribution combines a multiclass error-estimation framework with a practical filtering method, and the reported evaluation supports the usefulness of that combination.
neurips-2009-optimizing-multi-class-spat.tldr: A multiclass Bayes-error estimate guides spatio-spectral EEG filter optimization, improving classification over earlier multiclass spatial-pattern methods in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis can be disrupted by heavily corrupted observations. This paper studies an idealized recovery problem in which an observed matrix is the sum of a low-rank matrix and a sparse error matrix. The errors may be arbitrarily large; the structural assumption is that relatively few entries are corrupted.

The authors prove that a simple convex program efficiently and exactly recovers most low-rank matrices for most error sign-and-support patterns. The qualification matters because the guarantee does not cover every possible matrix and corruption arrangement. The result permits rank to grow nearly proportionally to the observation dimension, up to a logarithmic factor, while the number of corrupted entries can grow proportionally to the matrix's total size.

The analysis also produces proportional-growth results for completing a low-rank matrix from a small fraction of its entries. Simulations and real-data examples support the theoretical findings and suggest computer-vision applications. The central insight is that low-rank structure and sparse corruption can be separated exactly under the stated qualified recovery result, even when individual errors are very large.
neurips-2009-robust-principal-component-.tldr: A convex program exactly recovers most low-rank matrices under most sparse corruption patterns, even when corrupted values are arbitrarily large.

paragraphs: Online learning algorithms process information through a sequence of updates. They have strong convergence properties for risk minimization and convex games, including very large problems. This paper focuses on a computational obstacle: a design that depends on successive updates is inherently sequential, which makes it difficult to take advantage of multicore hardware.

The authors analyze online learning when updates are delayed. Such a delay separates the availability of an update from the moment when the algorithm can use it. The central question is whether this weaker timing arrangement preserves useful convergence behavior. Their result proves that online learning with delayed updates can still converge well.

This matters because accepting delayed updates facilitates parallel online learning. Computation can be organized around a less restrictive update schedule while retaining a theoretical basis for progress toward the learning objective. The title captures this tradeoff: slower arrival of individual updates can enable a more parallel learning process. The stated contribution is the convergence analysis that supports this computational possibility.
neurips-2009-slow-learners-are-fast-6640.tldr: Online learning can retain good convergence with delayed updates, providing a theoretical basis for parallel execution.

paragraphs: Speaker comparison estimates how similar the speakers in two speech recordings are, supporting verification, clustering, and identification. This paper treats comparison geometrically: features from each recording adapt a Gaussian mixture model, and the comparison is then performed in the space of those adapted models. The model parameters become the objects being compared.

The authors introduce inner product discriminant functions, or IPDFs, which use inner products between Gaussian-mixture parameter vectors. Linear transformations of these vectors compensate for nuisance variation. The framework extends support vector machines, joint factor analysis, and linear scoring, showing that many existing speaker-comparison techniques can be understood as relatively small variations within a shared representation.

This unified view also yields new scoring methods. On a 2006 NIST speaker-recognition evaluation task, the authors report excellent error rates with significantly less computation than existing techniques. The result links conceptual simplification with practical efficiency: expressing compensation and comparison through parameter transformations and inner products provides both a way to relate methods and a basis for developing new ones.
neurips-2009-speaker-comparison-with-inn.tldr: A shared inner-product framework unifies speaker-comparison techniques and produces new scoring methods with strong reported accuracy and lower computation.

paragraphs: Listwise ranking methods optimize an ordering of an entire set of objects, while applications such as information retrieval often care most about the first few positions. This paper asks whether existing listwise methods are statistically consistent for that top-k objective. The issue is whether optimizing their training losses aligns with the desired ranking risk.

The authors define a framework whose true loss and associated risks are based on top-k subgroups of permutations. It includes the earlier whole-permutation framework as a special case. Within this formulation, they derive sufficient conditions for consistency and describe how to modify existing surrogate losses so that they meet those conditions.

The contribution is both analytical and practical. It provides a way to assess whether a listwise training objective fits a top-k goal, then offers a constructive route to improving that fit. Experiments show that the modified methods can perform significantly better than their original versions. The theoretical conditions are sufficient guarantees, while the performance gains are findings from the reported evaluations.
neurips-2009-statistical-consistency-of-.tldr: A top-k ranking framework yields sufficient consistency conditions and loss modifications that improve existing methods in experiments.

paragraphs: A central idea in early-vision research is that visual representations reflect the statistical structure of natural scenes. Earlier versions of this idea explain Gabor-like receptive fields and modulation by nearby visual input, but the authors argue that they capture only part of the surrounding context. This paper develops a broader statistical account of those contextual interactions.

The proposed approximate model represents both linear and nonlinear correlations among responses of spatially distributed Gabor-like receptive fields. Training on natural scenes lets the model connect patterns of visual input with relationships among these responses. Its purpose is to bring several spatial context effects into one statistical framework.

The full model accounts for neural surround data from primary visual cortex and fits observations of the tilt illusion. It also supplies a statistical foundation for perceptual phenomena associated with the hypothesis that this cortical area constructs a saliency map. These findings show how one model can connect neural and perceptual effects through natural-scene statistics, while retaining the stated status of an approximate model and a hypothesis-based interpretation.
neurips-2009-statistical-models-of-linea.tldr: A natural-scene model of linear and nonlinear visual context accounts for several neural and perceptual effects within one framework.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples to have labeled from a pool of unlabeled data. This paper studies whether that choice reduces the number of labels needed when noise is present, the agnostic setting. The authors emphasize that the benefit depends on the problem and hypothesis space: some problems offer no advantage to any active-learning algorithm.

The paper gives sufficient conditions under which active learning is strictly better than passive supervised learning. The conditions concern noise, the classification boundary, and the underlying input distribution. Under the stated noise condition, finite-order smoothness of both the boundary and distribution yields a polynomial improvement in label complexity.

When the boundary and distribution are infinitely smooth, the reported improvement becomes exponential. This distinguishes two levels of regularity and their consequences for the value of selective labeling. The results identify settings where active learning has a provable advantage; they do not claim that smoothness is necessary or that every noisy classification problem benefits. Their significance is a conditional explanation of when label selection can substantially reduce supervision.
neurips-2009-sufficient-conditions-for-a.tldr: Under stated noise and smoothness conditions, agnostic active learning achieves polynomial or exponential label-complexity improvements over passive learning.

paragraphs: Separating several moving bodies requires grouping point trajectories according to their underlying motions. Spurious tracks and tracking mistakes make this difficult. This paper approaches the task through candidate subspaces estimated from the data, drawing on robust statistical model fitting to generate plausible explanations of trajectory structure.

The authors encode these hypotheses in a Mercer kernel rather than simply ranking the candidate models. The kernel expresses how plausibly two trajectories could come from the same subspace. This pairwise representation lets established statistical learning methods support outlier rejection, estimation of the number of motions, and segmentation of the trajectories.

The method is reported to work well even with severe outliers caused by false trajectories or mistracking. Experiments on Hopkins 155 report advantages over the compared state-of-the-art methods in motion-count recovery, segmentation accuracy, robustness to gross outliers, and computational efficiency. The central contribution is the way candidate model information becomes a similarity function, allowing multiple parts of the segmentation problem to use a common representation.
neurips-2009-the-ordered-residual-kernel.tldr: A kernel built from candidate motion subspaces supports robust trajectory grouping, outlier rejection, and automatic motion-count estimation.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to discover regions of the Internet associated with malicious activity as those regions change over time. The authors formulate the task as adaptive pruning of a known decision tree. Choosing a pruning means selecting a representation at an appropriate level of detail, rather than retaining the full tree.

Two difficulties shape the algorithm: the underlying tree has more than four billion leaves, and the target being tracked changes. The proposed method combines several experts algorithms with online paging algorithms. This combination addresses adaptation and space requirements together, which is essential when a full representation is too large and a fixed summary would become outdated.

The authors prove performance guarantees relative to the best possible pruning of a similar size. That comparison evaluates the method against a representation with a comparable space scale. Experiments on large real-world datasets report high accuracy and significant improvements over existing approaches. The work therefore combines a dynamic detection formulation, a space-conscious online algorithm, and both theoretical and empirical support.
neurips-2009-tracking-dynamic-sources-of.tldr: An adaptive tree-pruning algorithm tracks changing malicious Internet regions with guarantees relative to similarly sized prunings and strong reported accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to select a smaller set of features while preserving a useful guarantee for k-means clustering. The selection is unsupervised, so it does not require class labels. The proposed randomized algorithm chooses existing features and rescales them, producing a reduced representation on which a clustering algorithm can operate.

For an accuracy parameter epsilon between zero and one, the number of selected features is on the order of k log(k/epsilon) divided by epsilon squared. This bound depends on the requested number of clusters and the accuracy parameter, rather than the dataset's original feature dimension. It makes explicit how demanding a tighter accuracy setting affects the representation size.

The guarantee also accounts for the clustering algorithm used afterward. If that algorithm is a gamma-approximation, the selected features allow a partition with approximation factor 1 + (1 + epsilon) gamma, with high probability. The result therefore quantifies how randomized feature reduction and approximate clustering compose. It supports a reduced-feature workflow while explicitly tracking the resulting quality bound.
neurips-2009-unsupervised-feature-select.tldr: Randomized feature selection and rescaling reduce dimensionality while preserving a high-probability approximation guarantee for subsequent k-means clustering.

paragraphs: The nested Chinese restaurant process is a nonparametric Bayesian model for learning tree-shaped hierarchies from data. Its posterior distribution is intractable, so learning requires an inference method that can handle uncertainty over possible structures. The authors note that existing methods had relied on Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling.

This paper develops a variational alternative. To make that possible, the authors derive a tree-based stick-breaking construction of the mixture model. This provides a representation suited to the new inference procedure. Their variational algorithm efficiently explores a posterior over a large collection of combinatorial structures, addressing the challenge of reasoning over many possible hierarchies.

The method is demonstrated on text and handwritten-digit modeling, and the authors show that the nested Chinese restaurant process can also be adapted to continuous data. The contribution is thus a new computational route for hierarchical Bayesian modeling, supported by a representation that enables variational inference. The applications illustrate its use across different data types while retaining the tree-based structure at the center of the model.
neurips-2009-variational-inference-for-t.tldr: A tree-based stick-breaking construction enables variational inference for the nested Chinese restaurant process, with text and handwritten-digit applications.
